children.text: A one-dimensional colloidal particle obeys \(M\dot v=-\gamma v+F(t)+F_{ext}(t)\). Random molecular collisions supply impulses. In A, Fext=0. In B, approximate its velocity by independent constants vn on intervals \((n-1)\delta<t\le n\delta\), with zero mean and \(\langle v_nv_m\rangle=C\delta_{nm}\). Initially x=v=0. For C a dilute suspension of positive charge Q flows in a narrow channel of cross-section A. Neglect particle interactions, walls, background ions and gravity. A field E points along x. The diffusion flux is \(J_D=-D\,dn/dx\), the drift flux is JQ=nu, and osmotic pressure is Π=nkT with k=R/NA. For D a spherical particle has a=5.0 μm in water of viscosity η=\(8.9\times10^{-4}\) Pa s at T=25°C. Use γ=6πaη and R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Required experimental plots are reproduced below.
A collision at t0 supplies impulse I0 to a resting particle. Determine v0 and τ in \(v(t)=v_0e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}\).
Impulses Ii occur at ti after t=0. Find v(t) and specify which collision times contribute.
At t=Nδ find the mean displacement and its mean square in terms of C, δ and t.
For a finite nonzero Brownian mean square as δ tends to zero, find α and β in C∝δα and MSD∝tβ.

statement.text:
Characterization of soil colloids
A one-dimensional colloidal particle obeys \(M\dot v=-\gamma v+F(t)+F_{ext}(t)\). Random molecular collisions supply impulses. In A, Fext=0. In B, approximate its velocity by independent constants vn on intervals \((n-1)\delta<t\le n\delta\), with zero mean and \(\langle v_nv_m\rangle=C\delta_{nm}\). Initially x=v=0. For C a dilute suspension of positive charge Q flows in a narrow channel of cross-section A. Neglect particle interactions, walls, background ions and gravity. A field E points along x. The diffusion flux is \(J_D=-D\,dn/dx\), the drift flux is JQ=nu, and osmotic pressure is Π=nkT with k=R/NA. For D a spherical particle has a=5.0 μm in water of viscosity η=\(8.9\times10^{-4}\) Pa s at T=25°C. Use γ=6πaη and R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Required experimental plots are reproduced below.
a.1. Single impulse
A collision at t0 supplies impulse I0 to a resting particle. Determine v0 and τ in \(v(t)=v_0e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}\).
a.2. Successive collisions
Impulses Ii occur at ti after t=0. Find v(t) and specify which collision times contribute.
b.1. Displacement moments
At t=Nδ find the mean displacement and its mean square in terms of C, δ and t.
b.2. Continuum scaling
For a finite nonzero Brownian mean square as δ tends to zero, find α and β in C∝δα and MSD∝tβ.
c.1. Right-going crossing rate

Half the particles have speed +v and half −v. Linearize n(x) about x0. Find N+(x0), the right-going number crossing per area per time, using n0=n(x0) and s=dn/dx at x0.
c.2. Diffusion coefficient
Use the analogous N− and ⟨v²⟩=C to find JD, D and the MSD.
c.3. Osmotic balance
For the stationary concentration under E, balance osmotic forces on a slice of width Δx. Find dn/dx in terms of n, Q, E, k and T.
c.4. Drift velocity
With Fext=QE, zero mean initial velocity and ⟨F⟩=0, find ⟨v(t)⟩ and terminal velocity u.
c.5. Einstein relation
Use JD+JQ=0 to express D in terms of k, T and γ.
d.1. Experimental Avogadro estimate

Using the histogram of displacements sampled at Δt=60 s, estimate NA to two significant digits. Do not use a known value of k or NA.
d.2. Drift crossover
Replace each vn by u+vn. Find the MSD, its small- and large-time power laws, the crossover t*, and sketch a log-log plot.
d.3. Swimming microbes

A microbe swims at randomly selected velocity ±u0 for independent intervals δ0, in addition to Brownian motion. The supplied MSD plot has three regimes. Express each power law using D, u0, δ0 and t.
e.1. Coagulation threshold
Two colloidal particles interact through \(U(d)=-A/d+B\epsilon(kT)^2e^{-d/\lambda}/q^2\), with A,B>0, dielectric constant ε, ion charges ±q, and \(\lambda=\sqrt{\epsilon kT/(2N_Aq^2c)}\). Neglect thermal fluctuations and assume instantaneous terminal motion. Find the lowest salt concentration c that guarantees coagulation.

children.text: Integrate through the collision to obtain Mv0=I0. Afterwards Mdv/dt=−γv. Thus \(v_0=I_0/M\) and \(\tau=M/\gamma\). The field checks τ.
Linearity permits superposition: \[v(t)=\sum_{0<t_i<t}\frac{I_i}{M}e^{-(t-t_i)/\tau}.\] At an impulse include the instantaneous velocity jump Ii/M if using a right-continuous convention.

Write Δx=δΣvn. Each mean vanishes and every cross correlation vanishes. Therefore \(\langle\Delta x\rangle=0\) and \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=N C\delta^2=C\delta t\). The field checks the mean square.
The product Cδ must remain finite. Hence α=−1 and β=1.
Only particles between x0−vδ and x0 cross. Thus \(N_+=\frac1{2\delta}\int_{x_0-v\delta}^{x_0}[n_0+s(x-x_0)]dx=n_0v/2-sv^2\delta/4\).
\(N_-=n_0v/2+sv^2\delta/4\), giving \(J_D=-sC\delta/2\). Therefore \(D=C\delta/2\) and \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=2Dt\). The field checks D.
Force balance is Π(x)A+nAΔxQE=Π(x+Δx)A. Since Π=nkT, \(dn/dx=nQE/(kT)\).
The mean obeys \(M d\langle v\rangle/dt=-\gamma\langle v\rangle+QE\). Thus \(\langle v\rangle=(QE/\gamma)(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) and \(u=QE/\gamma\). The field checks u.
Substitute C3 and u=QE/γ into −Ddn/dx+nu=0. Cancelling nQE gives \(D=kT/\gamma\).

Take the frequency-weighted mean square of the histogram, approximately 6.34 μm². Since \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=RT\Delta t/(3\pi a\eta N_A)\), obtain \(N_A\simeq5.6\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). This is the estimate from these data, not the modern defined constant.

The nonzero mean adds a squared drift term: \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=u^2t^2+2Dt\). The terms match at \(t_*=2D/u^2\). The log-log slope rises from 1 at t≪t* to 2 at t≫t*. Draw continuous asymptotes meeting near t*.

If 2D/u0²≪δ0, the successive laws are \(2Dt\) for t≪2D/u0², \(u_0^2t^2\) for 2D/u0²≪t≪δ0, and \(u_0^2\delta_0t\) for t≫δ0. More exactly the last coefficient is u0²δ0+2D. The assumed intermediate regime makes its Brownian contribution negligible. The source solution labels this item D.1 in its prose, but its answer box and question identify D.3.

Under overdamped deterministic motion every repulsive-force interval must disappear. The threshold satisfies U′=U″=0, giving d=2λ and \(\lambda=e^2Aq^2/[4B\epsilon(kT)^2]\), where e is Euler's number. Hence \[c=\frac{8B^2\epsilon^3(kT)^5}{e^4N_AA^2q^6}.\] Setting only the potential barrier height to zero would not eliminate the force barrier and does not meet the stated deterministic criterion. The value above is the critical concentration, an infimum for finite-time coagulation from initially separated particles. At equality the force has a double zero at \(d=2\lambda\), approached only asymptotically in this overdamped model. Finite-time passage requires \(c>c_{\rm crit}\).
